open_obligations: Check that Irving et al.'s complexity model (polynomial-time judge, PSPACE via alternating debate moves) is the analogy the authors mean, and not a different complexity argument in that paper
Confirm that the citing paper offers no formal result, so the link should not be read as a theorem-level extension
in.other_title: Leike et al. apply Irving et al.'s complexity-theory analogy to recursive reward modeling
in.rationale: The authors take the complexity analogy that Irving et al. introduced for debate (polynomial-time judge, alternating moves) and re-apply it to their own recursive reward modeling scheme, mapping recursion depth to quantifier alternations. That is building on the cited framework with a stated change, so EXTENDS; no theorem is proved here.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Whether a polynomial-time evaluator can supervise harder problems through recursion or interaction; holds only as an analogy, with the user's evaluation treated as a binary polynomial-time predicate

open_obligations: Read p29 L1-10 to confirm the authors' mapping of critique recognition to Sigma_2^P and of n-step recursive reward modeling to the n-th level of the hierarchy
Check that the mapping is consistent with Irving et al.'s statement of how n-step debate corresponds to the polynomial hierarchy
in.other_title: Saunders et al. apply Irving et al.'s proof-system analogy for debate to argue critiques are natural assistance
in.rationale: Irving et al. model debate with a polynomial-time judge and unbounded debaters and relate n-step debate to the polynomial hierarchy; the authors adopt this framework and extend it to critiques and recursive reward modeling. The extension is an argument, not a theorem.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Complexity-theoretic justification for assistance schemes; holds only as an analogy, with humans as polynomial-time verifiers.

open_obligations: Check that the gain applies only to computations with polynomial-length human-verifiable transcripts, as the authors concede at p9 L33-L46, whereas Irving et al.'s unbounded model reaches all of PSPACE
Confirm that the definition at p5 L25-L28 ('The original definition of debate requires Vtime to be polynomial in n, but allows Ptime to be unbounded') matches Irving et al.'s formal model
in.other_title: Brown-Cohen et al.'s doubly-efficient debate gives Irving et al.'s debate a poly-time honest prover
in.rationale: The authors build directly on Irving et al.'s complexity model of debate (polynomial-time judge, unbounded provers) and state the change: the honest prover is restricted to polynomial time while the dishonest prover stays unbounded. This is a protocol-level extension, so EXTENDS.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Theoretical power of debate with a limited verifier; the change holds for computations with a polynomial-length human-verifiable transcript

open_obligations: Check whether the NEXP-with-cross-examination result the passage attributes to Irving et al. (2018) is in that paper or in Barnes & Christiano (2020)
Confirm the target record's complexity model (polynomial-time judge, unbounded debaters) is the assumption the passage calls unrealistic
in.other_title: Buhl et al. call the unbounded-debater assumption behind Irving et al.'s complexity results unrealistic
in.rationale: The authors do not dispute the theorem but argue its key assumption (unbounded debaters) is unrealistic for their purposes, a critique of the assumption without new data. They pair the claim with NEXP and cross-examination while citing only Irving et al., whose main theorem is stated for PSPACE.
in.scope: proposed CRITIQUES: Whether debate's complexity-theoretic guarantees carry over to computationally bounded debaters; holds as a critique of the unbounded-debater assumption only

open_obligations: Check that Irving et al. (2018) indeed assume computationally unbounded (optimal-play) debaters in the PSPACE result the critique refers to
Check that the 'as per the introduction' remark refers to the complexity model and not to a different part of the 2018 proposal
in.other_title: Brown-Cohen et al. call Irving et al.'s assumption of computationally unbounded debaters too strong
in.rationale: Irving et al. model debate with a polynomial-time judge and computationally unbounded debaters; the authors call this assumption too strong and measure debater complexity relative to each other instead. This is an argument about a modeling assumption with no new data on it, so CRITIQUES rather than CHALLENGES.
in.scope: proposed CRITIQUES: Whether debate guarantees should assume unbounded debaters; holds for the theoretical model of debate, not empirical LLM debate

text: For the complexity analogy the authors replace the human judge with an arbitrary polynomial-time algorithm H that outputs one bit (whether a statement is true), and allow the ML models arbitrary computational power so that the only limitation is the supervision signal. Using H to answer questions directly corresponds to the class P and to supervised learning.
title: Complexity model of debate: polynomial-time judge, computationally unbounded debaters
